title: Dan Sullivan vs. Dan Sullivan: Can a Name Stop an Election?
description:
Alaska's 2026 U.S. Senate ballot has two candidates named Dan Sullivan: Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg. State election officials removed the second Dan in June; Alaska's courts put him back. Now the U.S. Justice Department has sued Alaska, asking that the result not be certified if the senator loses and votes for the other Dan could have changed the outcome. We explain the August primary numbers (Peltola 49.54%, Sen. Sullivan 41.40%, Daniel J. Sullivan 2.47%), how Alaska's ranked-choice voting works, what the lawsuit asks, and what each side says.

We don't pick political sides. We just count the facts.

Sources:
Al Jazeera, Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump's DOJ suing in Alaska? (Oct 24, 2026): https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/24/dan-sullivan-vs-dan-sullivan-why-is-trumps-doj-suing-in-alaska
AP via PBS NewsHour, Trump says he ordered DOJ lawsuit over Alaska Senate race (Oct 23, 2026): https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-files-lawsuit-to-block-possible-democratic-win-in-alaska-senate-race
Alaska's News Source, Trump sues to disqualify votes for Petersburg's Dan Sullivan (Oct 23, 2026): https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/10/23/trump-sues-disqualify-votes-petersburgs-dan-sullivan/

scenes.say: Picture it. You're in a voting booth in Alaska. You find the candidate you came for. Then you look one line down. And there he is again.
Two Dan Sullivans. Same name, same state, same Senate race. Dave has been staring at this ballot for eleven minutes.
And now the federal government has gone to court about it. It wants the power to freeze the result, but only if one of the Dans loses.
Today's question: can a name stop an election? Who are these two men, what does the lawsuit actually ask, and what do both sides say?
Dan number one. Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican senator. First elected in twenty fourteen, re-elected in twenty twenty, now asking for a third six-year term.
Before that, he was Alaska's attorney general and its commissioner of natural resources. A long résumé. A very common name.
Dan number two. Daniel J. Sullivan Junior. A retired elementary school teacher and former Forest Service worker from Petersburg, a small town in southeast Alaska.
He entered the race at the end of May. He's registered as a Republican too. Because of course he is.
Republicans say he's a plant, put in the race to pull votes away from the senator. He says he decided to run on his own.
And then there's the person both Dans are trying to beat: Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former congresswoman.
In twenty twenty-two, she became the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. House. She served one term.
There's also a fourth candidate, Gerald Heikes. He'd like you to know he exists. Nobody has the same name as him.
Now the numbers. Alaska held its open primary in August. Everyone runs on one list, and the top four go through.
Mary Peltola came first, with forty-nine point five four percent.
Senator Sullivan: forty-one point four zero percent. More than sixty-eight thousand votes.
And the other Dan Sullivan: four thousand one hundred and seven votes. Two point four seven percent.
Two and a half percent sounds tiny. Hold that thought. In a close race, tiny can be the whole story.
Why does it matter nationally? Republicans hold fifty-three of the hundred Senate seats. Democrats, plus two independents who vote with them, hold forty-seven.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. So every single seat gets watched like a pot of coffee at six a.m.
For context, Alaska has only about seven hundred and thirty-eight thousand people. But it still gets two senators, same as California.
So how did two Dans end up on one ballot? It started in June, when Alaska's Division of Elections removed the second Dan.
According to Alaska's News Source, officials gave four reasons. First: the name choice itself was meant to confuse voters.
Second, his party choice. Third, campaign imagery that looked like the senator's. Fourth, he used a consultant who had backed Peltola.
He fought back in court. A superior court sided with him. Then Alaska's Supreme Court agreed and put him back on the ballot.
The timing was tight. The ruling came one day before the state's deadline to print ballots. Somewhere, a printer sighed with relief.
At a hearing, the chief justice asked whether the state really had to list him as a Republican. Another justice answered: but he's registered.
So here is what the ballot says now. The senator: Sullivan, Dan S, Registered Republican, Incumbent.
The other one: Sullivan, Daniel J Junior. No party label at all. He's the only candidate on that list without one.
One political scientist at the University of Alaska Southeast, Glenn Wright, told Al Jazeera the ballots are, quote, super, super, super clear.
Another, Forrest Nabors at the University of Alaska Anchorage, said the similar names could swing a close race. Depending on who you ask.
To understand the lawsuit, you need one more thing: Alaska doesn't just pick one name. Voters rank the candidates. First choice, second, third.
If nobody gets more than half the first choices, the last-place candidate is knocked out.
Their ballots then move to each voter's next choice. Repeat, until two candidates are left, and one wins.
You don't have to rank everyone. So if you only pick one name, and that name gets knocked out, your ballot stops counting in later rounds.
Here's the key point for our two Dans. A Republican voter can rank the senator first and the other Dan second, or the other way around.
Either way, if the other Dan is eliminated, those ballots flow on to the next choice. Ranked choice was supposed to remove the spoiler effect.
The catch: that only works if voters actually rank more than one name. Otherwise a mistaken vote for the wrong Dan simply ends with him.
The senator's campaign has even posted a video explaining how to rank. Dave watched it twice. Then rewound the part with his own name in it.
Now, the lawsuit. On Thursday, October twenty-second, the U.S. Justice Department sued the state of Alaska and its election officials in federal court.
Its stated goal, in its own words: quote, to protect the integrity of the twenty twenty-six Senate election in Alaska.
What does it ask? Don't certify the result if the senator loses, and if the votes for the other Dan would have changed who won.
And then: investigate whether people who voted for Daniel J. Sullivan actually meant to vote for Dan S. Sullivan.
Which raises a fun puzzle. How exactly do you ask a secret ballot what it meant? Dave suggests a séance.
The case leans on the National Voter Registration Act, specifically its findings and purposes section.
The President said he ordered it. He told reporters, quote, I'm the one that said do it.

items.text: "I'm the one that said do it"

scenes.say: Before that, he posted that powerful legal options were being considered to remove, his words, the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Junior from the ballot.
The Justice Department also points to Alaska's own election officials, who had found that the second Dan's campaign was an attempt to mislead voters.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said it was not the department's intention to, quote, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process.
He said the department would be unlikely to interfere outside of, quote, extreme circumstances.
Note the timing. The case was filed less than two weeks before Election Day, after ballots were printed, and after tens of thousands of Alaskans had already voted early.
So, the reactions. And yes, every side gets a turn at the microphone.
The second Dan called the lawsuit a, quote, gross misuse of the Justice Department, and said the courts had already settled it.
He also said the Division of Elections did, his words, a notable job of differentiating the two candidates.
Peltola's spokesperson called it a despicable political threat to overturn an election. The Democratic Senate campaign committee called it a sham.
The senator's own campaign kept it short: quote, we'll let the DOJ complaint run its course. It didn't say whether he supports it.
Alaska's other senator, Lisa Murkowski, also a Republican, said the department should never have filed this lawsuit.
Legal scholars are sceptical. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller called the argument, quote, so absurdly thin, and said the court will likely dismiss it.
Nabors, at the University of Alaska Anchorage, called federal intervention unusual, but said it could be justified if an election is run unfairly.
And it's not the first strange Alaska Senate race. In twenty ten, Murkowski won a write-in campaign by more than ten thousand votes.
Two sides, then. One says: two near-identical names can trick voters, so check before you certify. The other says: the ballot is clear, the courts ruled, let the count stand.
We don't pick a winner here. We just count the facts.
So what happens next? Election Day is Tuesday, November third. In Alaska, the full ranked-choice count can take weeks.
A judge will decide whether the lawsuit goes anywhere. Muller expects it to be dismissed next month. No court has ordered Alaska to pause anything.
The Justice Department can ask a court to step in. It cannot stop certification on its own.
And if the race isn't close? Then the whole question probably goes away. The lawsuit only matters if the other Dan's votes are bigger than the gap.
There's also a ballot question in Alaska that would repeal ranked-choice voting itself. So the counting system is on the ballot too.
Quick recap. Two men named Dan Sullivan are on Alaska's Senate ballot. One is the senator. One is a retired teacher. The courts let both run.
The Justice Department now asks a court to hold the result if the senator loses narrowly. Critics, including a Republican senator, call that wrong.
Voters decide on November third. Then the counting, and maybe the court, decide the rest.
As for Dave, he's finally ranked his choices. He then filled in a name-tag for himself, just in case there's another Dave on his street.
Your turn. Should ballots add more details, like a photo or a hometown, when two candidates share a name? Tell us in the comments.
If this helped, subscribe for calm, stick-figure news. See you at the next one.
